text: The sheepdog had taken its place on the rise, where the whole flock lay within sight. From there, it could see the gap by the gate. The sheepdog lies still as the flock gathers, and one ewe lingers near that gap. There is room for her to move either way. If the flock keeps moving, the sheepdog may have to rise and meet its weight. For you, that may be a choice held open a little longer, or one that begins to demand your strength.

The sheepdog chose this ridge long ago, high enough that no part of the flock falls out of sight. Nothing came at the sheep from behind while that watch was kept. Below, the flock is drifting apart into two grazings, one toward the river, one toward the higher grass, and neither has gone far enough yet to be the decision. The dog lies still and lets the shape of it come clear, because a body that moves too soon sees only what it has scattered. When the haunches gather, the whole weight of the animal goes into one line, and the ground it crosses is the ground it commits to. That gathering may be a strength in you still held back with the grazing unsettled, or a strength already leaning, waiting for the moment you name which way the flock goes.

Before you see anything, you hear the posts creak. A bull has turned in the pen, and the whole fence shifts with him. Uruz is strength too large for the space it was given. What stands around you now may be holding well and already leaning, both at once.

jm: Single Ehwaz (dva koně) · pojmenuj postavu · Opus
text: Behind the lead horse comes the second, still out of sight on the path below. When the first one tires, the second slows without being asked, and they come over the ridge together. Ehwaz is that agreement between two who move at one pace. Where you are going may hold both a shared stride and the wait it costs you.
